title: Atomisation and HTML: My Honest Journey Using AI to Plan Lessons Part 3
author: Dario Emanuele
summary: In the concluding chapter of his trilogy on AI-assisted lesson planning, Dario Emanuele declares the Sunday-night slide-deck struggle over after abandoning slide design entirely in favour of AI-generated HTML 'Interactive Webpages.' He diagnoses the unsustainable 'Frankenstein lesson' problem — teachers spending hours collaging questions, diagrams and definitions from multiple browser tabs — and describes hitting a wall because AI-generated slides broke formatting and looked terrible. His breakthrough was banning the word 'Slide' from his prompts: AI writes robust, interactive, offline-capable HTML far better than it designs slides, complete with reveal-answer buttons and drawing canvases. He shares a full copy-paste prompt workflow (retrieval, I Do/We Do/You Do, mini-whiteboard questions, printable PDF worksheets, plenary) that collapses planning from two hours to two minutes, letting him focus on pedagogy rather than delivery mechanics. He flags one remaining challenge: refining the atomisation process so the AI breaks concepts down without creating 'lethal mutations.'
points: The unsustainable 'Frankenstein lesson' problem — hours spent collaging resources from multiple tabs — is a driver of teacher burnout and attrition.
The breakthrough was banning the word 'Slide' from prompts and asking AI to build 'Interactive Webpages' (HTML) instead, which AI produces far more reliably.
HTML lessons are robust, interactive (reveal-answer buttons, drawing canvases) and work offline in a single file.
A copy-paste prompt sequence — retrieval, I Do/We Do/You Do, mini-whiteboard questions, printable PDF worksheet, plenary — cuts planning from about two hours to two minutes.
The remaining challenge is refining atomisation so the AI breaks concepts down without creating 'lethal mutations' that miss the deep structure.
quotes: We ask them to master behaviour management, explanation, and assessment, while simultaneously expecting them to build lesson resources
You spend an hour copy-pasting, cropping, and aligning text boxes. You are essentially creating a “Frankenstein” collage of a lesson.
I realised that Gemini (and other tools like notebookLM) struggles with the structural rigidity of “Google Slides.” The function calls often glitch.
It works offline: A single HTML file can store your entire lesson, Retrieval, Explanation, and Practice, without needing Wi-Fi.
I have stopped “designing.” I no longer worry about font sizes or aligning images. I focus entirely on the pedagogy
My next challenge is refining the Atomisation process within the AI to ensure it breaks down concepts correctly without creating what we call “lethal mutations
